## Simple explanation

XML is a text format that uses nested tags to describe structured data. It is
human-readable and can represent hierarchies such as a document with sections
and items.

## Technical explanation

Extensible Markup Language defines syntax for elements, attributes, and text
content. XML schemas can describe permitted structure and types. Namespaces
help avoid naming collisions. Parsers must handle encoding and external
entities safely; untrusted XML should be parsed with secure settings.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

XML remains common in configuration, data exchange, document formats, and
legacy systems that AI pipelines may need to ingest. Its explicit structure
can be useful, but malformed or unsafe parsing can break processing or expose
systems to attacks.

## How it works

A parser reads a document's tags and builds an element tree or event stream.
Applications validate that structure, extract needed values, and transform
the data into an internal representation.

## Practical example

An ingestion service can parse XML product records, validate required fields,
and convert them into a normalized schema before model feature generation.
Reject malformed records and disable unsafe external entity resolution.

## Common misconceptions

- XML is a syntax, not a database or a semantic model; the application must
  define what elements mean.
- Well-formed XML is not necessarily valid against a schema or safe to parse.
